On Gmail spam filtering: one user found it frustrating that Google already seems to block mail from relatively new domains, yet obvious spam messages still get through.

A user who had just been complaining about the Gmail web app's interface hoped a real Gmail API would let developers build better interfaces on top, to improve inbox management and cut time spent sifting through email.

Gmail doesn't implement IMAP properly: IDLE only signals new messages, not changes in unread count. After moving from self-hosted Dovecot, the user was shocked that read status didn't propagate across devices until a manual poll.

A developer spent a year trying to replicate Gmail's interface in a desktop app (BetterInbox) over IMAP and said IMAP is completely unsuited to the Gmail paradigm. The new API would have made their lives much easier.

One developer's IMAP client code for Google Apps Gmail was 'full of hacks to convert internal ids to Gmail ids and format conversion issues'. They welcomed replacing it with a couple of HTTP calls via the Gmail API.
A user is very reluctant to give any third party access to their Gmail mailbox, because most sites allow password reset by email, so it's like handing over the keys to the castle.
Gmail API auth scopes already allow read-only access, but one user wants to restrict apps to a specific label or subfolder for better security without forwarding mail.
SMS Backup+ to Gmail has been 'fantastic for archiving all of my texts'. Each message is stored with the contact as sender, and the user can search everything relatively easily.
Workaround for Google's OAuth restrictions: GSuite admins can whitelist existing apps. The user did this for SMS Backup+ so it keeps working, but noted consumer Gmail users probably lack that option.
Facing Google's restrictions on third-party apps, one user stopped backing up to Google and instead synced SMS Backup to a local Dovecot IMAP server. Setup turned out to be incredibly simple.
A user said Google restricting seamless third-party integrations hurts utility and was 'just another reason I'm happy with moving my primary mail to FastMail on my own domain.'
Google lets anyone register my gmail address as their 'alternative recovery email' without confirmation, so I periodically get a dozen 'recover your account' emails from strangers' accounts.

A user with a fairly generic gmail address has hundreds of accounts linked to it that they never signed up for, because people mistype or don't know their own address. The account became unusable, so they switched to their own domain about a decade ago.

Gmail's AI is surprisingly bad at filtering obvious spam: many messages arrive from unknown senders on fairly new domains, ending with lines like "if this isn't relevant, say 'not now'". The user is considering services that make senders confirm they're human.
"Tab to improve" is infuriating. The user has their own voice and deliberately uses some 'bad' writing tropes for effect. For them, "Tab to improve" is effectively "tab to delete my own personality".

A user's elderly mother saw what looked like a supermarket delivery email with the wrong date and thought her memory was failing. It was actually a Gmail AI summary that had hallucinated a different delivery date. The user disabled the AI features.
At work they use Google Workspace and saw all these AI features appear, but they were able to turn them off and haven't been bothered since. The process wasn't hard.

One user accepts about 50% of Gmail's improvement suggestions. Because it understands context, it catches correctly spelled but wrong words and sometimes makes sentences clearer. Sometimes it turns a warm email into a cold, strictly-business one, and those suggestions get ignored.

Google aggressively pushes Gemini with 'Write with AI' buttons everywhere. To use any of these features you must fully opt in to Smart Features across Google Workspace, which this user doesn't want to do.

One user left Gmail when Google reneged on free grandfathered custom-domain inboxes. They switched to iCloud+ at €0.99/month, which includes 50GB of storage, Private Relay and Hide My Email. No regrets so far.

Streak used the new Gmail API to build email snoozing. They found it really nice to use and much easier than IMAP. Building a full client is hard because listing threads doesn't return the messages, so participants and timestamps aren't available.

The API scopes allow only full control, read everything, everything except delete, or drafts access. There is no fine-grained control for third-party apps, which this user called insane from a security standpoint.

A developer tried to publish a Gmail add-on and failed because of the lockdown. Apps needing read access must pass a third-party security assessment costing about $75,000 per year, which they say blocks small developers and new entrants.
Gmail's own data export tools don't work at all for large inboxes (100GB+), so third-party tools are the only way to actually back up or migrate email.

Google's pushes to turn off 'less secure app access' grew obnoxious, including a 'prevented suspicious login' alert after a getmail run. The user is leaving: 'If I can't download it with POP or IMAP, then it's not email.'

Because dots don't matter in Gmail addresses, one user receives a stranger's commercial HVAC account, appointments and a lake house down-payment receipt. They wish Gmail could bounce mail that doesn't match their dot pattern.
Workaround: Gmail lets you filter in a dot-sensitive way. Mail missing the user's dot goes to a 'wrongguy' folder, which is mostly spam.

Several users like the dot-insensitivity. One uses dot variants as aliases when sites reject '+' addresses. Another says dot aliases are better than plus-labels because a leaker can't trivially strip them.

One user was told to 'try again later' every day for three weeks from the same IP they always used. They moved all services to another account; months later Gmail suddenly let them in. They will never again use Gmail for critical things.
Enabling 2FA with Google Authenticator and keeping backup codes safe means fewer 'soft AI' barriers to logging in. The user advises not relying on a phone number as the second factor.
Workaround: after waiting a couple of weeks and connecting via VPN to their previous country of residence, a user regained access with the recovery email. It took over 4 months to figure out.
During the outage, Gmail showed 'temporarily unavailable' (Numeric Code 93) for many users, including paid Google Apps accounts, while the Apps Status Dashboard still showed green.
One user recently switched from Gmail to Fastmail for $90 a year to avoid snooping and ad tracking, and couldn't be happier.
